title: Toxic Pain-Relief Residue Found on a 600-Year-Old Doctor's Tools
mediaSource: Ming dynasty doctor Xia Quan medical instruments aconitum residue archaeology

scenes.title: A toxic plant compound was found on 600-year-old surgical tools
scenes.narration: Tweezers and scissors from the tomb of a Ming Dynasty doctor in China contained residue linked to highly toxic Aconitum plants.

scenes.title: The tools belonged to physician Xia Quan
scenes.narration: The instruments were buried with a doctor named Xia Quan in Jiangsu Province in the early fifteenth century, a rare archaeological medical kit.

scenes.title: Aconitum residue remained on the metal
scenes.narration: Chemical analysis detected compounds associated with Aconitum, also known as monkshood, a plant famous for its powerful toxicity.

scenes.title: Ancient texts describe it as a topical anesthetic
scenes.narration: Historical Chinese medical texts say Aconitum powder could be applied to reduce pain before making surgical incisions.

scenes.title: The tools may provide rare direct evidence
scenes.narration: Texts described the practice, but finding the chemical residue on medical instruments offers unusual archaeological evidence that it may have been used during procedures.

scenes.title: Poison and medicine can be separated by how they are used
scenes.narration: A highly toxic plant may also have served as a pain-relieving medical substance. These small tools are revealing how surgery may have been practiced six centuries ago.
